sections.body:
A school bag is the bag that carries your school things from home to school and back. In English we call it a **backpack** or a **school bag**. In Vietnam it is a **cặp sách** or a **ba lô**.

A bag has different parts. The **main compartment** holds your books and notebooks. The **front pocket** is for small things, like a pencil case or a key. The **side pocket** often holds a water bottle. Some bags have a **zip pocket** inside, for money or a small note from home.

A school bag has to be light, because you carry it every day. A heavy bag makes your shoulders and back hurt. It can also make you lean forward and slouch, and slouching is bad for your spine, the long column of bones in your back.

Most children in Vietnam carry books, a notebook, a pencil case, a water bottle and a lunch box. Some carry an extra shirt, a hat or a raincoat.

A good bag is not the biggest bag. It is the bag that holds what you need, in good order, without pressing everything flat.
examples: This is my school bag for tomorrow.
The notebook goes in the main compartment.
My water bottle goes in the side pocket.
sections.heading: What a school bag is, and why it matters

sections.body:
Let us look inside a school bag piece by piece.

Books are the biggest things. A big book goes flat at the bottom, so it does not bend. Smaller books go on top of it.

A **notebook** is for writing. Keep it flat and dry, and put a cover on it.

A **pencil case** holds your pencils, pens, rubbers and ruler. A sharp pencil writes neatly. A **rubber** takes away mistakes. A **ruler** draws straight lines.

A **lunch box** holds your food for the school break. It should be easy to clean. A **water bottle** holds your drink, and it should always have a lid.

Some things come and go. A **homework sheet** goes in for today and comes home again. A **library book** comes back on the day it is due.

And a small thing that helps a lot: a **name label** on everything. If you lose a pencil, the teacher can find out whose it is.
examples: The big book goes flat at the bottom.
I keep my ruler in the pencil case.
I put a name label on my lunch box.
sections.heading: The things that live inside your bag

sections.body:
The weight of your bag matters more than most people think.

Children should carry a bag that is not too heavy. A good rule for a school child is a bag of about 10 % of their body weight. A child who weighs 30 kg should carry about 3 kg.

A heavy bag pulls you forward. Your neck and shoulders get tired, and you begin to slouch. A slouching child gets headaches more easily and finds it hard to sit straight in class.

The way you pack changes the weight. Put the heavy things close to your back, not far away. Use every pocket, so nothing hangs outside. Keep your water bottle full, but fill it at home, not at school.

Wear both straps. A bag on one shoulder pushes you to one side. Two straps spread the weight across both shoulders.

And check your bag at the end of the day. Take out the rubbish, take out the empty bottle, and take out anything you do not need tomorrow. A bag you empty stays light.
examples: My bag is too heavy when I put all the books on one side.
I use both straps so my shoulders feel better.
I take the empty bottle out of my bag every day.
sections.heading: Why a light bag is a good bag

sections.body:
These are the words for the things in your school bag. Learn them and you can ask for what you need at the shop.

A **backpack** is a bag with two straps that you carry on your back.

A **pencil case** is a small bag or box that holds your pencils, pens and rubbers.

A **notebook** is a book of blank pages for writing. In Vietnamese we call it a **vở**.

A **water bottle** is a container with a lid that holds your drink for the day.

A **lunch box** is a box that carries the food you eat at school. In Vietnamese it is a **hộp cơm** or a **cặp cơm**.

Try saying each word out loud and pointing to the thing in your own bag. Words stick when you use them with your hands.
examples: My backpack is next to the door.
The pencil case is in the front pocket.
Where is my lunch box? It is in the bag.
sections.heading: The school bag words, one by one

terms.example: My backpack has two wide straps.
terms.gloss: A bag with two straps that you carry on your back to school.

terms.example: My pencil case is the blue one.
terms.gloss: A small bag or box that holds your pencils, pens, rubbers and ruler.

terms.example: I write my homework in a notebook.
terms.gloss: A book of blank pages you write in at school.

terms.example: I fill my water bottle at home.
terms.gloss: A container with a lid that holds your drink for the whole day.

terms.example: My lunch box has rice and chicken in it.
terms.gloss: A box that carries the food you eat at the school break.

sections.body:
Packing the night before is calm. Packing it in the morning is a race. Here is the order that works.

First, look at tomorrow's timetable. Find out which books you need.

Next, take out yesterday's homework. Put the finished paper in your folder or on the desk, ready to hand in.

Then pack the big things. The big book goes flat at the bottom, close to your back.

After that, pack the small things. Pencil case, water bottle, lunch box, and the sheet of paper you were given.

Now the last check. Look at the table and look inside the bag. Is there anything on the table that belongs in the bag? Is there anything in the bag that does not belong there?

Finally, hang the bag on the door handle. In the morning you will not forget it, because you cannot leave without passing it.
examples: I check the timetable before I pack.
The homework goes in the folder.
I hang my bag on the door so I do not forget it.
sections.heading: How to pack your bag the night before
steps: Read the timetable and find the books you need.
Take out yesterday's homework and put it in your folder.
Pack the big book flat at the bottom.
Pack the pencil case, bottle, lunch box and papers.
Check the table and the bag one more time.
Hang the bag on the door handle.

sections.body:
Things break faster than you expect, but a little care keeps them for years.

Water is the enemy of books. If your bottle leaks, the paper goes soft and the ink runs. Close the lid tight, and keep the bottle upright in the side pocket.

Never write on the pages of a book with a pen. Use a pencil, so you can rub it out. If you spill something on a page, tell your teacher straight away.

Do not scribble on other people's books or bags. If you borrow a pencil, give it back.

Sharp things go in the pencil case, not loose in the bag. A loose pencil can poke through the bag and hurt someone's back.

And do not leave your bag on a chair or on the floor in a public place. Keep it with you or hold it between your legs. If a bag is lost, tell a teacher the same day, and say what is inside it, so people do not take the wrong things.
examples: I close my bottle lid so the books stay dry.
I borrow a pencil and give it back.
I tell the teacher at once if I lose my bag.
sections.heading: Looking after your bag and your things

item.summary: Your school bag carries your day with you. After reading this, you can name what is inside, pack it the night before, and take care of your things so they last.
item.title: My School Bag and What's Inside
